problem.description: Three different tests, across two different files, have each failed exactly once during a full `pytest tests/ -q` run, but all pass instantly and reliably when run in isolation or when the full suite re-runs under normal load. Not a regression from any specific change -- observed across Task 1.6/1.10/1.9 PM reviews, on unrelated commits/files. Low priority (does not block any task, always passes on retry) but worth root-causing before it erodes trust in a red CI run.
symptoms: tests/test_script_service.py::test_generate_script_exhausts_retries_raises failed once in a ~101s full-suite run, passed in isolation (0.29s) immediately after

tests/test_script_service.py::test_generate_script_backoff_sequence_is_1s_2s_4s failed once in a ~126s full-suite run (different session, unrelated Task 1.10 changes), passed in isolation (0.50s) immediately after

tests/test_youtube_service.py::test_generate_package_non_429_error_does_not_retry failed once in a ~305s full-suite run (unusually slow -- machine under heavy load), passed in isolation (0.50s) AND in a normal-speed full-suite re-run (~93s) immediately after
All three failing tests exercise a Gemini retry/backoff path (mocking asyncio.sleep to a no-op via an autouse `no_real_sleep` fixture), but now span two unrelated service modules/files, not just one

hypotheses.description: Test-order/fixture-scope leak: some other test running earlier in the full-suite ordering leaves global state (e.g. a module-level asyncio primitive similar to the _write_lock / _omnivoice_semaphore event-loop-binding class of bug already fixed twice this project) that only manifests when many tests share event loops in sequence, not in isolation.

System load / real wall-clock timing sensitivity: even though asyncio.sleep is mocked to a no-op, some other part of the retry loop (e.g. httpx client construction/teardown, or a real timeout somewhere) could be marginally timing-sensitive under the CPU/IO load of a many-test run (many of which spin up real uvicorn servers and Playwright browsers).

tests_run.command: pytest tests/ -q (3rd occurrence, in a session running many Playwright browsers concurrently)
tests_run.output: 1 failed (test_youtube_service.py::test_generate_package_non_429_error_does_not_retry), 349 passed in 305.13s -- notably slow vs the ~90-130s this suite normally takes

tests_run.command: pytest tests/ -q (immediate re-run, same machine, no code changes)
tests_run.output: 350 passed in 92.66s -- back to normal speed, zero failures

tests_run.command: pytest tests/ -q (4th occurrence, final verification pass for Task 1.6 Sub-task 1.6c -- unrelated frontend/speaker-route changes, no Gemini/script_service code touched)
tests_run.output: 1 failed (test_script_service.py::test_generate_script_backoff_sequence_is_1s_2s_4s -- same exact test as the 2nd occurrence, not just the same file), 387 passed in 243.88s -- again notably slower than the ~90-130s baseline

findings: All four incidents self-resolved on isolated or full-suite re-run with zero code changes.

The 3rd occurrence's evidence favors hypothesis 2 over hypothesis 1: the failing test is in a completely different file/module from the first two occurrences (test_youtube_service.py vs test_script_service.py) -- a state leak from one specific preceding test (hypothesis 1) would more plausibly recur in the same file/fixture context, not jump modules. The correlation with an unusually slow run (305s vs the normal ~90-130s) directly supports load-based timing sensitivity (hypothesis 2).

The 4th occurrence again correlates with an unusually slow full-suite run (243.88s), a second independent data point supporting hypothesis 2 (system load), and happened on a change set (Task 1.6 Sub-task 1.6c: new frontend page + a project_service/speakers route) that touches nothing in script_service.py, gemini retry logic, or asyncio.sleep mocking -- ruling out a regression from that specific work.
Not blocking: every PM review so far has verified the specific failure is pre-existing/unrelated to the change under review before accepting it.

resolution.root_cause: Not fully confirmed, but evidence now favors system-load-induced timing sensitivity (hypothesis 2) over cross-test state leakage (hypothesis 1) -- see findings. Two of four occurrences correlate with a full-suite run notably slower than the ~90-130s baseline.
resolution.verification: 4 occurrences now, all self-resolving on isolation/retry, none blocking, none tied to the change under review each time. Per the standing recommendation after the 3rd occurrence, downgrading this to a documented known-flaky-under-load note (see TRACKER.md Known Issues) rather than continuing open investigation -- closing this session as a known, accepted, low-priority flake. Reopen only if it starts failing in isolation (not just under full-suite load) or blocks an actual task.
